EVOLUTION THROUGH PARTICLE TRAFFIC

Install on your phone for app-style access.
Completed runs are cached in this browser. Export downloads a portable copy.

Evolution controls

Evolve a full tile field to minimize particle collisions. Each genome encodes one tile shape per cell.

Shared particle trial

Every candidate gets the same injection times and edge positions. All cells are occupied. Collisions consume the pair and mutate that tile during the trial; offspring inherit the starting layout.

Trials use a compiled C / WebAssembly engine in a background worker, with no real-time waits. Evolution and replay use the same simulation core. Unchanged genomes reuse their exact previous result. Only the winning replay runs at viewing speed. Selection uses collision count alone. Fast exits can win. This is optimization for this traffic trial, not a guarantee for every possible input.

THE ARCFIELD FIELD GUIDE

Small rules. Evolving routes.

How to run experiments, understand the measurements, and compare what evolution discovers.

No matching sections. Try “collision,” “seed,” “fit,” or “export.”

1. Quick start

Arcfield searches for tile layouts that produce fewer particle collisions. You choose an experiment, a genetic algorithm tests many layouts, and the site shows the best layout’s particle behavior. The live journal and landscape reveal the search as it runs.

  1. Keep the default settings for a first experiment, or choose 12 × 9 for a smaller field. For a quick test of the workflow, try 20 generations and a population of 12.
  2. Press Evolve the field. Look for the worker’s configuration acknowledgement, named phase, and percentage progress.
  3. Watch the best/average collision graph and the fitness landscape as candidate trials finish. The tile canvas stays hidden during the search.
  4. When the experiment finishes, the winner’s field appears and its trial replays automatically. Use Replay trial to watch the same inputs again.
  5. Use Export experiment ZIP to keep the data. Completed runs are also cached in this browser.
  6. Change the experiment seed or one control, run again, then enable Compare saved runs to inspect both experiments together.

This guide can stay open while the search runs. Use the contents links, the jump menu, or search to find a topic. Press Escape or the × button to close it. The question-mark keyboard key opens the guide when you are not typing in a form field.

2. Tiles and particle physics

Each candidate is a rectangular field with a tile in every cell. The genome is simply the list of tile types. Current experiments evolve complete starting layouts; there is no separate tile-growth phase.

TileConnectionsParticle behavior
Arc A · type 0North–East and South–WestTwo independent quarter-circle paths.
Arc B · type 1North–West and East–SouthThe alternative quarter-circle pairing.
Cross · type 2North–South and East–WestParticles travel straight through; perpendicular traffic can collide.

Paths meet at the midpoint of a shared tile edge. A particle follows its incoming path forward, rather than choosing a new direction at a crossing. Leaving the outer boundary removes the particle and counts an exit. There are no empty cells to fall through in the current model.

A straight traversal is one tile length. A quarter-circle traversal has radius half a tile and length π/4, approximately 0.785 tile lengths. Speed is measured along the actual path, so a curve takes less time to traverse than a straight crossing.

At each simulation step, a collision is detected when particle centers are less than 0.21 tile lengths apart. Both particles are consumed. The impacted tile changes to one of its other two types using a seeded random choice. Subsequent traffic encounters that new route. A brief flash marks the impact in the replay. When several possible collisions occur in a step, a stable pair order resolves them.

The engine advances at 60 fixed simulation steps per simulated second. It is a discrete computational model, rather than an exact continuous marble-physics solver. Its routing and collision rules define the system you are exploring.

3. Seeds and particle trials

The experiment seed makes the starting population, evolutionary choices, edge-entry positions, and collision-induced tile changes reproducible within the same application and simulation version.

Particles enter at regular intervals set by the injection rate. The positions are random: the generator chooses one of the four sides, then a cell along that side. Every candidate in a run gets the same injection schedule, speed, and trial horizon. This makes their collision scores directly comparable.

The trial ends at the configured horizon. Particles still in transit at that point do not continue to accrue collisions afterward. A longer horizon gives traffic more time to interact; a higher injection rate adds more traffic. Changing either one changes the optimization problem.

Simulation seconds are not real waiting seconds. The background engine advances them as quickly as the processor permits. Only the visible winner replay is paced for watching. Two different seeds can produce different traffic schedules as well as different evolutionary searches. Comparing seeds therefore tests both kinds of variation together; it does not isolate just the initial population.

4. Every experiment control

ControlMeaning and tradeoff
Run name · optional, up to 80 charactersA readable label for history, plots, results, and exports. If blank, the seed is used. The name does not change randomness or fitness.
Experiment seedText identifying the deterministic random streams. Repeat the same complete configuration to reproduce a run on the same version.
Generations · 1–1,000How many populations are evaluated. The default is 300. More generations allow more search, but improvement can plateau.
Population · 4–100Layouts tested per generation. A larger population explores more alternatives and requires more evaluations.
Mutation per tile · 0–100%Independent chance that an offspring tile changes to one of the other tile types. Low values preserve structure; high values disrupt more of the inherited layout. This is distinct from collision-induced tile changes during a trial.
Elite survivors · 1–20The best starting layouts copied unchanged into the next population. This must be smaller than the population. Elitism preserves good solutions.
Tournament size · 2–10Number of randomly drawn contestants considered for each parent selection. The lowest-collision contestant wins. Larger tournaments increase selection pressure.
Field resolution12 × 9, 16 × 12, or 24 × 18 cells. Larger fields mean longer genomes and more possible layouts. The grid fills the same visible canvas.
Trial horizon · 5–120 secondsSimulated duration of each candidate’s trial. Longer horizons reveal later interactions and cost more computation.
Particles injected per second · 1–30Regular injection frequency, with seeded random entry locations. The number scheduled is horizon × rate.
Particle speed · 1–10 tile lengths/secondDistance traveled along paths per simulated second. It changes encounter timing and how quickly particles can exit.

For a controlled comparison, change one setting at a time. Keep the seed and particle-trial settings fixed when investigating mutation or selection. Keep the trial settings fixed when interpreting collision-count differences between runs.

5. How evolution works

  1. Create a population. The seed generates random complete tile fields.
  2. Evaluate each starting layout. Run the shared particle trial and count collisions. Tile changes caused by impacts belong to this trial’s temporary state.
  3. Rank the layouts. Fewer collisions is better. The site keeps the best observed starting genome.
  4. Preserve elites. Copy the configured number of top layouts unchanged.
  5. Select parents. Run a tournament for each parent. Contestants are sampled with replacement, so a layout can be drawn more than once.
  6. Cross over and mutate. Take one parent’s genome and replace a contiguous interval of its flattened tile list with the other parent’s values. Independently mutate tiles at the chosen probability. Fill the rest of the next population with these offspring.
  7. Repeat. Evaluate the next generation until the configured total is reached, then reveal the winner.

Offspring inherit the parents’ starting genomes, not their collision-mutated final fields. Evolution across generations and rewiring within a trial are two separate processes.

Unchanged genomes can reuse their exact cached score for that run’s fixed trial. A cache hit is still an evaluated population member; it does not require a fresh simulation. This evaluation cache is separate from the browser’s saved-run history.

The fitness objective is collision count alone. Average path length and short exits help explain outcomes, but they do not affect selection. A layout can win by routing particles quickly back out. Zero collisions is the minimum possible score, and further improvements cannot appear below zero.

6. Progress, journal, and worker

The simulation is written in C and compiled to WebAssembly. It runs in a background browser worker on your device. It uses fixed simulation buffers and no real-time waits. Evolution and replay use the same compiled core.

The worker acknowledges receiving the experiment, then reports phases such as downloading/compiling the engine, creating the population, evaluating particle trials, ranking, and tournament selection/breeding. Overall percentage tracks the search. Candidate and trial percentages provide a more detailed view within a generation.

A five-second heartbeat reports the latest phase. The page also checks for replies and reports when it has not heard from the worker. Timers can be delayed when the browser or operating system suspends a background tab. An animated indicator alone is not proof of progress; use acknowledgements, advancing counts, and actual replies.

Best collisions
The lowest collision count found so far. With deterministic trials and elitism, this should not get worse across generations.
Population average
Average collisions among the current generation’s candidates. It can rise even when the best result is preserved.
Unique layouts
Number of distinct starting genomes in that population. Low diversity suggests the population has become similar; it does not prove the search is finished.
Generations since improvement
How long it has been since a strictly lower best score was found. Ties do not reset this counter.

The journal records candidate scores, cached results, tournaments, offspring, mutations, and generation summaries. Turn off Follow latest to read earlier entries. The visible journal is capped at 2,500 entries; the full candidate measurements are still captured for export.

The evolution graph shows best-so-far and population-average collisions by generation. Throughput reports distinguish actual simulated trials from reused results. A simulation-speed multiplier compares accumulated simulated time with real elapsed time; it is not a change to particle speed.

Cancel search stops the worker. You can export the observations collected so far, but a canceled run does not reveal or automatically save a completed winner.

7. Reading the fitness landscape

The landscape is a scatter plot of evaluated observations. Its three coordinates connect starting-field geometry to measured particle behavior:

AxisDefinition
Mean path lengthMean full geometric length of boundary-connected routes in the starting layout, averaged over boundary entry ports. Straight traversals contribute 1; curves contribute π/4.
Short exit routesNumber of distinct boundary-to-boundary routes that exit within the selected number of tile visits. Each route is counted once in either direction.
Collisions · vertical in 3DCollisions observed in the dynamic trial, including its tile changes. Lower means fitter under the current objective.

Short exits are the “closed edges” idea made measurable. A route can take a particle from the perimeter back to the perimeter after only one or a few traversals, offering less time in the field. Use the 1–8 tile threshold to explore this. A tile visit is not the same unit as geometric path length: a curved visit is shorter than a straight visit.

Enclosed internal loops that cannot be entered from the outer boundary are excluded from these route statistics. The topology describes the initial genome. It does not measure the average actual distance traveled by all particles during the collision-mutating trial.

Drag to orbit the 3D plot, use the scroll wheel to zoom, or focus the canvas and use arrow keys to rotate. Reset view restores the camera. Click or tap a dot to inspect its generation, candidate, score, path length, and short exits.

Projection switches to 2D views: collisions versus path length, collisions versus short exits, or path length versus short exits. The last view has no collision axis; inspect a point for its score. Generation slice shows all observations or only the latest generation in point-only mode.

The live plot retains a deterministic sample of up to 1,600 observations per run, plus the best result if needed. The latest-generation view retains that whole population. Sampling keeps drawing responsive; exports and fitted statistics use all recorded candidate observations. Cached/repeated evaluations can occupy the same position.

One run uses generation colors. Comparing multiple runs uses distinct run colors and winner markers. This is a measured projection of a much larger search space: layouts with identical plotted coordinates can still have different internal structures.

8. Best-fit lines and comparisons

Enable Compare saved runs, select the runs in the history list, and choose Point clouds, Best-fit lines to winners, or Points + fitted lines. Each selected run gets its own color and winner marker. A new live run can appear alongside earlier completed runs.

Each line is an orthogonal least-squares fit constrained to pass through that run’s winner. In plain terms, the site finds the direction through the winner that minimizes the cloud’s squared perpendicular distances from the line. The three coordinates are normalized by the shared plot ranges before fitting, so their different numerical units do not automatically determine the direction.

The fit includes all recorded candidate observations, including repeated/cached evaluations, rather than just the sampled dots. Its displayed segment ends at the winner, extends toward higher collision values, and is clipped to the shared plotting box. Changing selected runs or the short-exit threshold can change the shared scaling and fitted directions.

The legend reports how much of the winner-anchored spread lies along the fitted direction. A large fraction means a straight line captures much of that spread; a small fraction means the cloud is less line-shaped. This number is not a standard regression R². A zero-spread cloud has no meaningful line extent.

The fitted line is a statistical summary, not the path evolution took. Use the generation graph and journal to inspect chronological improvements. Generation slicing is disabled when fitted lines are displayed because the fit uses the entire run.

For meaningful collision comparisons, use the same field size, horizon, injection rate, and speed. Mixed configurations can be displayed together, but scores remain raw counts, not normalized difficulty ratings. Run labels include grid size and settings context so you can identify differences.

9. Winner and collision replay

After all generations finish, the winner’s initial field appears and the shared particle trial replays. Watch particles follow curves, exit the perimeter, and rewire tiles when they collide. Replay trial restarts from the same initial genome and seeded inputs; it does not continue evolving.

The headline values show the winner’s total collisions, collisions divided by trial seconds, particles that exited, and current replay time. The displayed replay time advances independently of how long the background search took. Some particles may still be inside when the trial horizon ends.

The winner collision graph shows either counts in one-second bins or their cumulative total. Its vertical marker tracks the replay’s current simulated time. The full trace is already known from evaluation, so the graph can show the full horizon before the replay has visually reached it.

At completion, the replay checks its collision count against the evaluated score. A mismatch message indicates an unexpected inconsistency, rather than an evolutionary improvement. Loading a saved result restores that run’s winner and inputs for replay.

10. Saved runs and browser storage

Successful completed experiments are saved automatically in this browser using IndexedDB. The cache contains full captured export data, the winner and its replay inputs, generation history, plot samples, and fitting statistics. The latest completed experiment is restored after a refresh.

Give a run a name before starting, or use Rename beside a saved run. Names appear in comparisons and export filenames; renaming does not change the seed or simulation. Select checkboxes to include or exclude runs from comparison. Load result restores an earlier run’s winner, experiment controls, replay, and downloadable data. Finish or cancel an active search before loading a saved result.

Use Delete beside a saved run to remove it, or Clear saved runs to remove all saved experiments. Both actions ask for confirmation. They remove the cached metrics, winner, and saved export data from this browser, but keep the PWA’s offline application files and any exports you already downloaded. A result currently on screen can still be viewed/exported until you start another run or refresh; an active experiment continues and may save its result afterward.

Saving can take a moment; the status line reports success or a storage error. If storage is unavailable or full, the completed result remains usable on the current page and can still be exported.

These records belong to this browser’s storage for this site. They are not synchronized to another device, another browser profile, or a backend account. Clearing site data removes them, and private browsing or browser eviction can limit retention. Download exports for a portable copy.

Running, canceled, and failed experiments are not automatically saved as completed historical runs. Their partial observations can be downloaded while the page remains open. Reloading during a search stops its worker.

11. Exporting and analyzing data

The header has two download buttons. Candidates CSV produces a spreadsheet-ready table of every recorded candidate observation. Export experiment ZIP packages the full current experiment. Load a saved result first to export an earlier run.

ZIP fileContents
settings.jsonSeed, complete experiment configuration, run status, metric definitions, timestamps, and export/application identifiers.
candidate_metrics.csvGeneration, candidate, page elapsed time, collisions, mean/max starting route length, boundary route count, all eight short-exit thresholds, and whether the result was cached.
generation_summary.csvBest, mean, worst, diversity, stagnation, breeding/mutation counts, and simulated/reused trial totals for completed generations.
winner.jsonThe winner’s initial genome, score, exit count, collision bins, topology metrics, settings, and best-score trace. Present after completion.
winner_tiles.csvWinner’s initial tile types with zero-based x/y coordinates. Present after completion.
winner_collisions.csvOne-second collision bins and cumulative totals. Present after completion.
README.txtSchema notes, tile connections, units, limitations, and partial-export interpretation.

Exports are independent of the plot’s visual sample and the journal’s display cap. A repeated/cached layout remains a row, so the table represents evaluated observations rather than only unique genomes. Intermediate candidate genomes and each candidate’s full collision time series are not retained.

You can export during a run or after canceling it. Such snapshots are labeled partial/running/canceled/failed as appropriate. An interrupted generation can have candidate rows without a completed generation summary. The CSV files use UTF-8 with a byte-order mark; the ZIP is a standard uncompressed archive.

Tile coordinates increase rightward in x and downward in y. The exported winner is the starting layout, not the final layout after replay collisions. Exact reproduction requires matching simulation and genetic-algorithm versions as well as the same inputs.

12. Installing and offline use

Arcfield can be installed as a progressive web app (PWA), giving it a home-screen icon and a standalone window. Open the site in your phone’s browser first and sign in if asked. The current site audience and access restrictions still apply.

  1. Android: open Arcfield in Chrome or another supporting browser, then tap Install app. If no prompt appears, open the browser menu and choose Install app or Add to Home screen.
  2. iPhone/iPad: open Arcfield in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen and Add. The app’s own button shows instructions when an automatic install prompt is unavailable.
  3. Embedded browsers: if you opened the link inside ChatGPT or another app and cannot find installation, use Open in browser first.

Wait for the offline-ready message while online. The app caches its interface, help, icons, and compiled simulation engine. After that setup, cached experiments and new local simulations can work offline. The first visit, authentication, and downloading updates need a connection. Browser storage policies can still remove offline files or saved runs; exports remain useful backups.

The offline shell is versioned as one coherent package. When an update is ready, use Update app after finishing or canceling an active search. The update button refuses to interrupt a running search. Applying an update reloads the page, so export partial data before canceling or refreshing. Completed runs stay in browser storage.

Installing does not move computation to a remote server or guarantee that the operating system will keep a hidden/locked app running. Keep the app open while an experiment runs. Depending on browser and platform, an installed app can have a separate storage context from another browser; saved runs are not synchronized between those contexts.

13. Questions and troubleshooting

Nothing seems to happen after Start.
Look for the acknowledgement that the worker received the configuration, then its phase and percentage. A missing-reply notice distinguishes silent startup from confirmed progress. Check any engine-download error; downloads time out after 15 seconds. Export any existing partial data before refreshing.
The search is slow.
Try a smaller field, fewer generations, a smaller population, a shorter horizon, or a lower injection rate. Total population evaluations are approximately generations × population, with exact-result reuse reducing actual simulations. Runtime depends on your device; a background worker moves work off the page’s UI thread, not onto a remote server.
The best score is flat.
A plateau can mean the same fitness keeps winning, diversity is low, or the current mutation/selection settings are not finding improvements. Inspect the population average and unique-layout count. If the best is already zero, it cannot decrease further under this objective.
Different runs have very different scores.
Check horizons, injection rates, speeds, field sizes, and seeds before attributing the difference to evolution. Different seeds also change the shared traffic schedule.
The fitted line is tiny or hard to see.
The cloud can have little spread, the fitted direction can be foreshortened by the camera, or clipping near the winner can shorten the displayed segment. Rotate, switch to a 2D projection, or choose Points + fitted lines to inspect the distribution.
The plot shows fewer dots than the exported row count.
The plot samples older observations to stay responsive. Repeated observations can also overlap. Exports include all captured rows.
My old runs are missing.
Check that you are using the same browser/profile/site. Site-data clearing, private browsing, unavailable storage, or quota failure can affect persistence. Exported ZIP/CSV files are independent copies; the current interface does not import them back into the run cache.
Can I open this guide without stopping a run?
Yes. Opening, searching, scrolling, and closing the guide do not cancel the worker. Device/browser scheduling can still affect the speed of any active computation.
